claims.text: In as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi films, the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis are governed by a broad distribution of local exchange interactions rather than by composition alone.
The broad distribution of local exchange interactions arises from defects and chemically inhomogeneous regions.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films contain a high density of defects and local chemical inhomogeneities.
Untreated as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films exhibit a sharp, highly hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
Mild post-deposition annealing reduces defect density.
Mild post-deposition annealing modifies grain-boundary characteristics.
Annealing produces more homogeneous local chemical order.
Low-dose ion irradiation can provide an effect equivalent to mild thermal annealing.
Annealing narrows the distribution of local exchange interaction energies.
Microstructural reordering induced by annealing homogenizes the magnetic exchange landscape.
A more homogeneous exchange landscape produces more distributed nucleation of the magnetostructural transition and broadens its temperature range.
A broader and less abrupt entropy-change feature reduces magnetocaloric hysteresis.
Annealed films will display a more gradual magnetic-entropy-change peak than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed films will have lower hysteretic losses than the as-deposited baseline under low applied fields.
The post-deposition treatment will improve heat-exchange rates.
The baseline films have limited heat-exchange efficacy because defects and inhomogeneities are concentrated.
The predictions apply over approximately 100–300 K under low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Over-annealing may cause grain coarsening that counteracts the proposed benefits.
X-ray diffraction peak FWHM can be used as a proxy for defect density and grain size.

contradictions.description: The initial broad exchange-interaction distribution and chemical inhomogeneity are said to produce a sharp transition, whereas annealing is said to narrow that distribution and increase homogeneity while producing a broader, more distributed transition. The hypothesis does not explain why narrowing the local-energy distribution should broaden rather than sharpen the transition.

Improved heat exchange is attributed to defect homogenization, while no change in film geometry, thermal conductivity, or surface-to-volume ratio is specified. The stated baseline limitation therefore does not connect coherently to the intervention.
